Working from a collection of rare and often nearly undocumented recordings, the project uncovers a forgotten culture of synthesizers, home studios, spirituality, landscape, and imagination. This mix offers a journey through that world, bringing together 15 recordings that reveal the remarkable breadth, intimacy, and imagination of this largely unmapped musical culture. Andy Boay :: Doomed Posted on October 1, 2026 October 1, 2026 Andy Boay returns with an opus crafted with ecstatic care: a journey of reverbed vocals and guitar noodles, a lo-fi love letter, a bedroom SMiLE , and its own thing completely: Doomed . Doomed shares the same creative DNA as its brilliant predecessor, 2025’s You Took That Walk For The Two Of Us : another painstakingly crafted cassette recording, with tape manipulation galore and self-harmonies aplenty. Jeremy Cunningham :: Passing Fires Posted on October 1, 2026 October 1, 2026 Jeremy Cunningham makes music that seems to be perpetually slipping out of its own frame. On Passing Fires , the Chicago drummer moves from free-jazz and skronk to electronics, funk, post-rock and pop, assembling a cast of improvisers, producers and singers who keep the music in motion. There are moments of muscular rhythmic interplay, strange electronic textures, children’s voices, whispered vocals and unexpected turns. It’s an album of restless curiosity, but never restlessness for its own sake: Cunningham’s drumming provides a steady gravitational pull as the music wanders. Transmissions :: Johnny Marr Posted on September 30, 2026 October 1, 2026 Certain people play guitar in a way that is immediately recognizable, no matter the context. Our guest this week on Transmissions, Johnny Marr, is one such guitarists. A founding member of legendary indie band The Smiths, his sound is undeniable a blend of jangle, chime, bite, and attitude. He’s back with a new album The Age Of Everything, which he joins us to discuss. Along the way, we also get into the global influence of The Smiths, discuss how Black American musicians inspired his sound, and share some of his less apparent influences, including Neil Young, who if you hear Marr tell it, played a rather pivotal role in the development of British punk rock. Style, sound, and the “politics” of guitar: Johnny Marr on Transmissions. Future Sounds Of Jazz Vol. 16 Posted on September 29, 2026 September 28, 2026 Future Sounds of Jazz Vol. 16 is both a forecast and a wormhole. Across two discs, Michael Reinboth and Michael Rütten move through jazz, dub, electronic music, improvisation, and psychedelia with the intuitive logic of a late-night DJ set. The result is a strange, elastic universe of DJ Oil, Bitchin Bajas, Booker Stardrum, Nico Zam, Ilhan Ersahin, and Momoko Gill—and a reminder that the future of jazz remains gloriously undefined. The hotel is coincidentally located in Anacita, a fictional coastal town created by Casey for 2017’s Relatives in Descent. It’s the kind of place where the “liberal-minded close their eyes and dream of technology and kombucha.” Lee Ranaldo :: Guitar-Centric Film Soundtracks Posted on September 28, 2026 September 28, 2026 As a member of Sonic Youth, Drift, and his many other musical detours, Lee Ranaldo has treated the guitar as a pure sound source, creating dynamic new expressions in rock & roll and the avant-garde alike. But Ranaldo’s new project, a soundtrack to director Joris Postema’s “eco-doc” The System, presents a new side of Lee, that of a filmic composer. To commemorate the album’s release, Ranaldo sent over notes about nine other guitar-centric soundtracks that serve as conceptual inspirations for The System. Here’s a look at 10 standout songs from Across the Horizon thus far — music that demonstrates the breadth of the series as a whole. Asher White :: Love Aggregates Posted on September 24, 2026 September 23, 2026 Asher White goes maximalist on Love Aggregates , building heavy doses of orchestral power pop from her bedroom. A fragmentary heartbreak album touching on dysphoria, precarious labor, Jerry Garcia, Citi Bikes, and Flatbush in the snow, it transforms intimate falsettos, arpeggiating guitars, and toy piano melodies into a luminous, redemptive vision of love. Those Were the Days of Miracle and Wonder :: Paul Simon’s Graceland at 40 Posted on September 24, 2026 September 24, 2026 Paul Simon’s 1986 album Graceland exists in this weird state, an album that eternally evokes 1986, but always sounds so different from other albums of its era. It’s an collection that’s self absorbed, but also so relatable when the listener finds themselves hitting middle age. It brought world music to the forefront, but also presented a misleading picture. It’s a fascinating study in contrast and now, some 40 years later it’s an album we still can’t make up our minds about even as we listen to it for the hundredth time.
